prompt: Which URI best follows REST conventions for fetching one order?

options.text: GET /getOrder?id=9001
GET /orders/9001
POST /orders/fetch
GET /order-service/mysql/9001

explanation: Resources are nouns with their own URI; the method says what to do. (a) puts the verb in the path. (c) uses POST for a read, which is neither safe nor cacheable. (d) leaks implementation details into the contract.

prompt: Which method is idempotent but NOT safe?

options.text: GET
POST
PUT
HEAD

explanation: PUT changes state, so it is not safe, but sending the same PUT twice leaves the same result. GET and HEAD are safe (and idempotent). POST is neither.

scenario: A mobile client sends POST /payments to charge $40. The connection times out before any response arrives. The client cannot tell whether the server processed it.

options.text: Retry the same POST at once; servers deduplicate identical POST bodies
Never retry; tell the user the payment failed and ask them to start over
Retry with the same idempotency key so the server can replay the result
Switch to a GET to check whether it ran, then POST again without a key

explanation: Retrying POST blindly can charge twice, and refusing to retry loses payments that never reached the server. An idempotency key lets the server recognise the retry and return the original result. (a) assumes deduplication that plain POST doesn't have. (b) may report a failure for a payment that went through. (d) races: the first request may still be in flight when you check.

prompt: A logged-in user tries to delete someone else's document. Which status code fits best?

options.text: 401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
400 Bad Request
500 Internal Server Error

explanation: The caller is authenticated but not permitted: 403. 401 means missing or invalid credentials. 400 is for malformed requests. 500 blames the server for a correct refusal.

prompt: Why is returning 200 OK with {"error": ...} in the body a bad idea?

options.text: JSON bodies can't represent errors, so clients fail to parse them
Clients, proxies, retries and monitoring read the status and see success
Error bodies on 200 are much larger, which hurts mobile bandwidth
HTTP forbids sending a response body together with a 200 status

explanation: Everything between client and server reads the status line: retry logic, caches, dashboards and alerts all treat a 200 as success, so failures get cached and go unalerted. JSON can describe errors fine, size isn't the problem, and 200 responses normally carry bodies.

prompt: What is the most likely cause?
scenario: A social feed uses GET /feed?limit=20&offset=20 for page 2. Users on busy days report seeing the same post at the bottom of one page and the top of the next.

options.text: The CDN is caching each page, so page 2 is served from an older copy
Offset paging: a new post at the top shifted every item down by one
The client re-sorts by ID, so items reorder between the two requests
The database is eventually consistent, so replicas return pages twice

explanation: With OFFSET, an insert while you page shifts every row, so the last item of page 1 becomes the first of page 2. Cursor pagination anchors on the last item seen. A cached page would be stale, not shifted by exactly one; client-side sorting and replica lag don't produce this repeat-at-the-boundary pattern on their own.

prompt: Why does cursor (keyset) pagination stay fast on deep pages?

options.text: It caches every page server-side, so deep pages are served from memory
With an index on the sort key, it seeks to the cursor; no rows skipped
It returns fewer rows per page, so each query does less work overall
It sends the cursor in a POST body, which avoids the query-string limit

explanation: WHERE (created_at, id) < (cursor) lets the index start at the right place, while OFFSET must read and discard every skipped row. Cursors don't rely on caching, page size is the same either way, and it works fine with GET.

prompt: Which are true of cursor pagination? Select all that apply.

options.text: It cannot jump directly to page 37
It needs a unique tie-breaker in the sort key
Cursors should be treated as opaque by clients
It is slower than offset for the first page

explanation: No random access (a); without a tie-breaker, rows with equal timestamps can be skipped (b); opaque cursors let you change the encoding later (c). (d) is false: the first page costs about the same either way.

prompt: Why should an API whitelist which fields can be sorted and filtered?

options.text: To shrink JSON responses by leaving the unused fields out
Each filter or sort needs an index; arbitrary ones cause scans
Because HTTP caps query strings at three parameters per URL
Because HATEOAS links can only point at whitelisted fields

explanation: Unindexed sorts and filters turn into full-table scans that can take a database down, so you only expose the ones you've indexed. Whitelisting doesn't change response size, HTTP has no three-parameter limit, and HATEOAS is unrelated.

prompt: Which change can you ship without a new API version?
scenario: Your public API returns user.name. Product wants to add the user's full legal name. Thousands of mobile apps that never update rely on the current response.

options.text: Rename name to full_name, since old clients already read that value
Add an optional full_name field next to name; clients ignore unknowns
Change name from a string to an object with first and legal parts
Make a previously optional field required so names are always set

explanation: Additive, optional changes don't break clients that ignore unknown fields. Renaming a field, changing its type and adding a new requirement all break existing clients that can't update.

prompt: What does HATEOAS add to a REST response?

options.text: An API version number in each body so clients detect changes
Links to related resources and the actions available next
A cache expiry for each resource so clients know when to refetch
A machine-readable error code alongside the HTTP status

explanation: HATEOAS (hypermedia as the engine of application state) adds links so clients discover what they can do next by following them. Versioning, cache headers and error codes are separate concerns. Most practical JSON APIs skip hypermedia and document URIs instead.
